paragraphs: Spatial observations often arrive as irregularly scattered points rather than a regular image or sequence. Their density can vary, and useful relationships may span both nearby and distant locations. This paper develops a transformer for such data, addressing the computational burden of comparing every point with every other point and the risk of overconfident predictions where observations are sparse.

The model organizes points into a quad-tree hierarchy and learns representations at multiple spatial resolutions. It uses coarse approximations to make spatial attention more efficient. This gives the architecture a way to represent relationships at different scales without relying entirely on expensive attention between individual points. A separate uncertainty branch estimates confidence associated with noisy input features and point sparsity.

The authors analyze computation and memory requirements and evaluate the model on real and synthetic datasets. They report better prediction accuracy than multiple baselines and demonstrate processing up to one million points on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. These results support the approach's practical scalability in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2023-a-hierarchical-spatial-tran.tldr: A hierarchical transformer uses multiscale spatial representations and approximate attention to process up to one million irregular points on one GPU.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object category also requires knowing when a similar object falls outside that category. This paper addresses that boundary problem in out-of-distribution detection using vision-language models. It develops automatically tuned descriptions that distinguish both clearly different categories and unfamiliar examples that closely resemble a recognized category.

The method learns two levels of context. Perceptual context separates the categories involved in the current task, such as cats and apples. Spurious context distinguishes a category from similar outsiders, such as cats and panthers. Together, these support a two-stage decision: identify a likely category, then assess whether the example actually belongs inside its boundary.

The resulting CATEX framework can expand its recognizable category set by merging contexts learned for different subtasks. Experiments support its effectiveness, robustness, and extensibility, including consistently large improvements over rivals across several ImageNet-1K protocols. The paper also offers insights into scaling prompts to thousands of categories and incorporating large language models into zero-shot applications. Its contribution combines more precise rejection decisions with a practical mechanism for extending recognition.
neurips-2023-category-extensible-out-of-.tldr: CATEX learns hierarchical category descriptions that reject similar outsiders and can be merged to recognize additional categories.

paragraphs: Combinatorial group testing seeks to identify a small active subset within a larger population through queries involving groups. This paper changes the problem by making the elements selfish agents. Each active agent chooses whether to participate in a query and wants its own identity to become learnable from the feedback as early as possible.

The authors study adaptive strategies under a solution concept called Adversarial Equilibrium. The central distinction is whether agents know k, the number of active agents among n total agents. When k is known, they construct equilibrium strategies with learning time O(k log(n/k)), which they establish as nearly optimal. Thus, strategic participation can still permit efficient identification in this information setting.

When k is unknown, the authors construct strategies taking time on the order of n to the power k and prove a lower bound of order n for any such strategies. These bounds leave a gap, but establish a strong separation from the known-k case. The results show how agents' incentives and information change the difficulty of group testing relative to its classical formulation.
neurips-2023-combinatorial-group-testing.tldr: Group testing with selfish agents admits nearly optimal equilibrium strategies when the active population size is known, but becomes substantially harder when it is unknown.

paragraphs: A continual learner needs to retain earlier knowledge while acquiring new knowledge. Compositionality adds another demand: familiar concepts should help it understand unfamiliar combinations. The paper argues that existing benchmarks do not adequately measure this ability, leaving uncertainty about whether continual learning methods build knowledge that can be recombined and transferred forward.

The authors introduce two vision benchmarks, Compositional GQA and Compositional OBJects365, together with Compositional Few-Shot Testing. Their evaluation covers systematicity, productivity, and substitutivity as distinct aspects of compositional generalization. This broadens assessment beyond whether a learner remembers previously encountered tasks, asking how useful its acquired concepts are for handling new compositions.

Experiments examine five baselines and two methods based on modularity. The results indicate somewhat favorable compositional abilities in the feature extractors learned by current continual learning methods. However, the findings also indicate that modular approaches require further development to improve compositional generalization. The main contribution is an evaluation framework that makes this capability more directly testable, alongside qualified evidence about what existing methods already achieve.
neurips-2023-does-continual-learning-mee.tldr: Two new benchmarks and a testing framework reveal some compositional ability in continual learners while highlighting room for better modular methods.

paragraphs: Understanding video captured from a person's viewpoint can require computationally expensive models. EgoDistill addresses this cost by combining information from a sparse set of video frames with head-motion measurements from an inertial measurement unit, or IMU. The aim is to preserve useful information from a heavy video model while requiring substantially less computation.

The approach uses distillation: it learns to reconstruct the video-clip features produced by the heavier model. Sparse frames supply semantic information about the scene, while lightweight IMU readings supply head-motion information. Their combination provides the inputs for reconstructing those features. The authors also introduce an IMU-based self-supervised pretraining strategy as another component of the method.

Evaluations on Ego4D and EPIC-KITCHENS show that EgoDistill outperforms the compared state-of-the-art efficient video-understanding methods. The paper reports requiring 200 times fewer GFLOPs than equivalent video models. This is a reduction in computational operations, and the stated findings support the value of combining visual semantics with motion measurements for efficient egocentric understanding. The result specifically concerns an approach that has access to both frames and IMU readings.
neurips-2023-egodistill-egocentric-head-.tldr: EgoDistill combines sparse video frames with IMU head-motion readings to reconstruct heavy video features using 200 times fewer GFLOPs.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate samples through an ordinary differential equation, which follows a deterministic probability flow, or a stochastic differential equation, which includes noise. Comparing these choices is difficult because data distributions, learned score errors, and numerical effects all influence results. This paper studies two limiting cases: zero diffusion and large diffusion.

The analysis first introduces an error concentrated in a short portion of the score function's trajectory, then extends the treatment to arbitrary errors. For the localized perturbation, timing matters. An error near the end of generation favors the ODE over an SDE with a large diffusion coefficient. An earlier perturbation favors the SDE, with the resulting generation error suppressed exponentially as the diffusion magnitude tends to infinity.

Numerical experiments on Gaussian, Gaussian-mixture, and Swiss-roll distributions, as well as MNIST and CIFAR-10, validate the reported phenomenon. The findings provide a conditional explanation of when stochasticity helps: its benefit depends on where score errors occur during generation. The comparison therefore identifies different favorable regimes for the two processes.
neurips-2023-exploring-the-optimal-choic.tldr: In the analyzed limits, stochastic generation better suppresses early score errors, while deterministic generation handles late perturbations better.

paragraphs: A generative model can produce convincing images while failing to generalize beyond its training examples. This makes evaluation more demanding than judging appearance alone. The paper identifies complementary weaknesses in existing measures: likelihood scores are not always applicable and rarely track perceptual fidelity, while sample-based scores such as FID can miss overfitting.

Feature Likelihood Divergence, or FLD, is a parametric score computed from samples using density estimation. It evaluates three qualities together: novelty relative to the training samples, fidelity, and diversity. Including novelty makes generalization an explicit part of the assessment. This matters because realistic and varied outputs can still leave unanswered whether a model has learned to produce examples beyond those it encountered during training.

The authors demonstrate empirically that FLD detects particular overfitting cases missed by previously proposed metrics. Evaluations across image datasets and model classes also show that it agrees with intuitions captured by metrics such as FID while providing a broader assessment. The evidence supports FLD as a more comprehensive evaluation tool in the tested settings.
neurips-2023-feature-likelihood-divergen.tldr: FLD evaluates generated samples for novelty, fidelity, and diversity, detecting overfitting cases that earlier metrics miss.

paragraphs: A graph neural network may perform differently on a new graph when its data distribution differs from the training graphs. If the new graph has no labels, directly measuring classification accuracy is unavailable. This paper studies how to estimate the performance of an already trained GNN under precisely that deployment condition.

The proposed framework has two stages. First, it constructs a DiscGraph set intended to represent a broad range of differences between graph distributions. Its discrepancy measure uses outputs from the GNN, including internal node representations and predicted node classes. Second, it uses supervision from that set to train GNNEvaluator to estimate the target GNN's node classification accuracy.

At inference time, the evaluator predicts performance on unseen graphs without requiring their labels. Experiments on real-world test graphs demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. The contribution is a learned assessment of a particular model's expected accuracy under graph distribution changes. This addresses uncertainty about deployment quality separately from the GNN's own task of assigning classes to nodes.
neurips-2023-gnnevaluator-evaluating-gnn.tldr: GNNEvaluator learns from diverse graph distribution differences to estimate a trained GNN's accuracy on unseen graphs without test labels.

paragraphs: Sequence models need to capture relationships across both short and long distances. Linear recurrent neural networks have attracted renewed interest as efficient models, but the paper argues that their gating mechanisms often emphasize outputs while overlooking forget gates inside the recurrence. HGRN makes those internal gates central to how information is retained.

The model gives each forget gate a learnable lower bound. These bounds increase monotonically through the network's layers. This arrangement allows upper layers to retain information for longer periods, while lower layers model more local, short-term dependencies. The hierarchy therefore organizes different layers around different temporal scales through a direct constraint on their forgetting behavior.

The authors evaluate HGRN on language modeling, image classification, and the Long Range Arena benchmarks, reporting evidence of both efficiency and effectiveness. These experiments support the usefulness of hierarchical forgetting across the tested tasks. The architectural contribution is a way to combine gated linear recurrence with a structured division between local processing and longer-term memory.
neurips-2023-hierarchically-gated-recurr.tldr: HGRN uses increasingly restrictive forget-gate bounds across layers to support local processing below and longer-term memory above.

paragraphs: Compressed search indexes make retrieval efficient on large collections, but compression can reduce accuracy in high-dimensional spaces. The paper also identifies a training problem: objectives may omit useful interactions between queries and documents. KDindex addresses both concerns by teaching a lightweight index to reproduce ranking information from a more accurate search model.

The teacher can be a high-precision approximate nearest-neighbor or maximum-inner-product search model, such as a graph-based index. The student receives supervision to preserve the teacher's ordering of the top-k relevant results. This supplies information about query-document relationships. Training also includes reconstruction loss and a strategy for balancing posting lists, helping avoid a trivial outcome in which every candidate is assigned to the same centroid.

Experiments show that KDindex outperforms existing learnable quantization-based indexes. The paper also reports an index that is 40 times lighter than the compared state-of-the-art non-exhaustive methods while maintaining comparable recall. The findings support transferring ranking behavior as a way to improve compressed retrieval without requiring the student to retain the teacher's larger index.
neurips-2023-knowledge-distillation-for-.tldr: KDindex distills accurate search rankings into compressed indexes, reporting comparable recall with an index 40 times lighter than the compared non-exhaustive methods.

paragraphs: Choosing a pretrained vision-language model depends on the intended task and dataset. Testing every candidate can require substantial computation and a labeled evaluation collection that is not yet available. This paper introduces a model-selection task designed for that earlier stage, when the application can be described in words but its downstream data cannot be accessed.

Language-Only Vision Model Selection, or LOVM, asks methods to use only a textual description of the desired application. They must perform two related jobs: rank candidate models and predict their zero-shot performance. Ranking addresses which model to choose, while performance prediction addresses how well a candidate is expected to work without task-specific training examples.

The authors provide a benchmark containing ground-truth evaluations of 35 pretrained vision-language models across 23 datasets. Those measurements supply reference outcomes against which language-only selection methods can be assessed. The contribution is the task definition and evaluation resource: it creates a concrete way to study model selection without requiring access to the downstream dataset at selection time.
neurips-2023-lovm-language-only-vision-m.tldr: LOVM benchmarks whether text descriptions alone can support ranking vision-language models and predicting their zero-shot performance.

paragraphs: Weak supervision combines imperfect signals to generate training labels, reducing dependence on manually established ground truth. Those signals can also introduce bias. The paper shows that a dataset capable of supporting a fair model with true labels can become arbitrarily unfair when labeled through weak supervision. This makes the labeling process itself a fairness concern.

The authors propose a model of unfairness in supervision sources and validate it empirically. They then develop a mitigation technique based on counterfactual fairness. Their theoretical analysis establishes that the approach can improve accuracy and fairness simultaneously. This is a possibility demonstrated by the analysis, rather than a guarantee that every application avoids tradeoffs.

Experiments report accuracy improvements of as much as 32% over weak-supervision baselines while reducing the demographic parity gap by 82.5%. An extension aimed at maximizing performance achieves state-of-the-art results on five of ten WRENCH datasets. Together, these findings indicate that correcting source bias can improve the quality of inferred labels in ways that benefit both predictive performance and measured fairness.
neurips-2023-mitigating-source-bias-for-.tldr: A counterfactual fairness technique mitigates bias in weak supervision and can improve accuracy and fairness together.

paragraphs: A bandit algorithm learns which actions yield high rewards while making decisions over time. This paper evaluates its performance using Nash regret: the difference between the unknown optimum and the geometric mean of expected rewards across rounds. Through its connection to Nash social welfare, this measure provides a principled way to express fairness across rounds.

The analysis assumes stochastic linear rewards that are nonnegative and sub-Poisson, a condition that includes bounded nonnegative rewards. For a finite action set in dimension d over T rounds, the authors obtain a bound scaling as the square root of d/T times log(T times the number of actions). They also give a bound for potentially infinite action sets, scaling as d to the power 5/4 times log(T), divided by the square root of T.

The algorithm builds on successive elimination, supported by tailored concentration bounds and geometric sampling techniques. The authors establish essentially tight upper bounds, showing that this stronger welfare-based objective admits rigorous learning guarantees under the stated reward assumptions.
neurips-2023-nash-regret-guarantees-for-.tldr: The paper gives essentially tight linear-bandit guarantees for Nash regret, a geometric-mean reward criterion that expresses fairness across rounds.

paragraphs: Multilingual translation training must decide how frequently to sample each translation direction. Increasing one direction's share might seem like a straightforward way to improve it. After training more than 200 models across model sizes, data sizes, and language directions, the authors find that giving a direction more weight does not always improve its performance.

With imbalanced training data, the tradeoff curve produced by weighting tasks can depart from the traditional Pareto front. This complicates efforts to improve all directions together. The authors propose a Double Power Law to predict the observed performance tradeoffs, reporting robustness across different languages, levels of data adequacy, and numbers of tasks.

They then use that predictive relationship to formulate sampling-ratio selection as an optimization problem. Experiments show better performance than temperature searching and gradient manipulation methods while using one fifth to one half of the total training budget. The practical contribution is a model of how sampling affects multilingual performance that can guide allocation more efficiently than the compared selection methods.
neurips-2023-on-the-pareto-front-of-mult.tldr: A Double Power Law models multilingual translation tradeoffs and guides sampling ratios more efficiently than the compared selection methods.

paragraphs: Online systems receive behavior from users over time, and some users may deliberately disrupt learning through actions such as fraudulent clicks or fake reviews. This paper studies two linked goals: learning effectively despite corrupted behavior and identifying the users responsible. It also asks how unknown relationships among users can help the system learn more efficiently.

The authors introduce the LOCUD problem and a bandit algorithm called RCLUB-WCU. The algorithm learns and uses user relations while accounting for potential corruption. A second algorithm, OCCUD, detects corrupted users using the relations inferred by RCLUB-WCU. The design therefore connects robust decision-making with ongoing detection rather than treating every user's behavior independently.

The authors prove a regret upper bound whose dependence on time asymptotically matches the lower bound up to logarithmic factors, and which matches existing results in degenerate cases. They also establish a detection-accuracy guarantee for OCCUD. Experiments report stronger performance than previous bandit algorithms and high detection accuracy, supporting the value of learning user relations in this setting.
neurips-2023-online-corrupted-user-detec.tldr: Two connected algorithms learn user relationships to support robust online decisions and detect corrupted users, with theoretical and empirical guarantees.

paragraphs: Actions in first-person video often combine a hand movement with an object. Even large datasets cover only a sparse set of these combinations and a limited set of objects. This paper introduces an open-vocabulary action-recognition task in which verbs learned during training must generalize to actions involving both previously seen and novel objects.

The method separates verb prediction from object prediction. An object-agnostic verb encoder models the action component, while a prompt-based object encoder uses CLIP representations to recognize an open vocabulary of interacting objects. This separation directly addresses the need to reuse a learned verb when the object involved changes, including when that object was absent from the training vocabulary.

The authors create benchmarks from EPIC-KITCHENS-100 and Assembly101. In these evaluations, closed-action methods fail to generalize, while the proposed method is effective. Its object encoder also significantly outperforms existing open-vocabulary visual-recognition methods on novel interacting objects. The results support treating action and object recognition separately for this specific generalization challenge.
neurips-2023-opening-the-vocabulary-of-e.tldr: Separating verb and object prediction helps first-person action recognition generalize learned verbs to previously unseen interacting objects.

paragraphs: Variational inequalities provide a framework for equilibrium and optimization problems, including certain games. This paper studies stochastic monotone problems with a separable structure, where the algorithm accesses noisy first-order information. Its main goal is to reach accurate solutions efficiently while exploiting the structure available in the problem.

The proposed stochastic accelerated gradient-extragradient algorithm, AG-EG, combines extragradient updates with Nesterov acceleration. For strongly monotone variational inequalities, the authors establish that the iterates stay within a bounded domain. They combine this property with scheduled restarting to prove an optimal convergence rate. The guarantee applies to the specified problem setting and its assumptions.

The paper also specializes the analysis to bilinearly coupled, strongly convex–strongly concave saddle-point problems, including bilinear games. In that setting, it obtains more detailed convergence rates matching the corresponding lower bounds. Randomness contributes an additive statistical-error term that is optimal up to a constant factor. These results explain how acceleration and extragradient methods can jointly achieve the best available rates within the analyzed classes.
neurips-2023-optimal-extragradient-based.tldr: AG-EG combines acceleration, extragradient updates, and restarting to achieve optimal convergence guarantees for the studied structured stochastic problems.

paragraphs: Developing financial language models requires task-specific training material and a consistent way to evaluate results. PIXIU brings those pieces together in an open framework containing an instruction dataset, a financial language model, and a benchmark. The paper addresses the lack of publicly available resources of these kinds identified by the authors.

The instruction dataset contains 128,000 samples covering varied financial tasks, document types, and data modalities. The authors use it to fine-tune LLaMA into FinMA, a model intended to follow instructions across financial tasks. Pairing the model with its training resource makes the approach available for further study and development.

The evaluation benchmark spans eight tasks and 15 datasets, including six financial language-processing tasks and two financial prediction tasks. The authors analyze FinMA alongside several existing language models to identify their respective strengths and weaknesses. The reported contribution is a shared basis for training and assessment, with the model, data, benchmark, and experimental results released openly. The abstract presents this comparative analysis without claiming that FinMA wins every task.
neurips-2023-pixiu-a-comprehensive-bench.tldr: PIXIU combines financial instruction data, the LLaMA-based FinMA model, and an eight-task benchmark into an open research framework.

paragraphs: Protein engineering involves searching a vast sequence space in which useful regions can be sparse and labeled measurements scarce. Practical design also often requires improving several properties together. ProteinNPT is a non-parametric transformer variant tailored to protein sequences, with particular emphasis on learning from limited labels and supporting multiple tasks.

The authors first study supervised prediction of protein fitness and properties. They develop several cross-validation schemes to support robust evaluation, reimplement previously strong baselines, and extend those baselines using ideas from different parts of protein-engineering research. This makes comparative assessment a substantial component of the work alongside the proposed architecture.

Across the evaluated protein-property tasks, ProteinNPT consistently outperforms all of those comparison methods. The authors then investigate iterative design through extensive computational experiments involving Bayesian optimization and conditional sampling. Those experiments demonstrate value for choosing and generating candidate sequences over repeated design steps. The findings connect stronger property prediction with usefulness in in silico design, within the label-scarce and multi-property challenges motivating the work.
neurips-2023-proteinnpt-improving-protei.tldr: ProteinNPT improves protein-property prediction over the evaluated baselines and shows value in computational experiments for iterative protein design.

paragraphs: Reaching a training optimum quickly and learning a model that generalizes are different objectives. This paper examines that distinction for Gauss–Newton optimization in over-parameterized, one-hidden-layer networks in the mean-field regime. It studies both convergence and implicit bias: how the optimization process influences the solution and features that emerge.

The theoretical result establishes global convergence in continuous time, with a faster rate than gradient descent because of improved conditioning. A synthetic regression study then examines generalization. Gauss–Newton consistently finds a global optimum faster, but good test performance appears when random initial weights have small variance and a small step size slows convergence.

The experiments also reveal what the authors call hidden learning. Under that setting, the network can acquire features with good generalization properties even while its overall training and test performance remains suboptimal because the linear layer is under-optimized. This separates the quality of learned features from the current quality of predictions. The study therefore exposes a tradeoff between rapid convergence and generalization in the investigated setting.
neurips-2023-rethinking-gauss-newton-for.tldr: Gauss–Newton converges quickly in the studied networks, but synthetic experiments show that slowing it can favor features and solutions that generalize better.

paragraphs: Vision transformers spend substantial computation on dense multiplications in attention and feed-forward layers. ShiftAddViT reparameterizes pretrained models using cheaper operations, including additions and bitwise shifts, to accelerate GPU inference without training from scratch. The authors implement and optimize custom kernels with TVM so that the proposed operations can translate into practical hardware benefits.

For attention, queries and keys are mapped to binary codes, and matrix multiplications among queries, keys, and values are replaced with additive kernels. The authors find that this preserves accuracy for the examined attention variants. Applying shift-based replacements to feed-forward layers, however, causes accuracy losses. They address this with a mixture of experts that includes both multiplication and shift operations.

A latency-aware balancing loss trains a router to distribute tokens among experts, assigning more work to faster experts in principle. Across the evaluated two- and three-dimensional vision tasks, ShiftAddViT achieves up to a 5.18-fold latency reduction and 42.9% energy savings with comparable accuracy. These results support adapting the operation mix to balance efficiency and predictive quality.
neurips-2023-shiftaddvit-mixture-of-mult.tldr: ShiftAddViT combines additions, shifts, and multiplication experts to reduce GPU latency and energy while retaining comparable accuracy in the evaluated vision tasks.

paragraphs: Neural-network robustness certifiers often need linear bounds on nonlinear activation functions. Tight bounds help these tools reason about network behavior, but existing constructions have relied heavily on manually designed solutions for familiar functions. This paper introduces a criterion for measuring bound tightness and a more general procedure for constructing bounds.

For functions convex within the region of interest, the criterion supports optimal bounds. For the broader class of functions that are Lipschitz-continuous in that region, SOL adaptively selects sample points and computes linear bounds within a chosen epsilon tolerance of optimal tightness. Adaptive sampling builds a representation suited to the particular function being bounded.

The theoretical worst-case runtime scales as epsilon to the power minus 2d, where d is the input dimension. The authors report substantially milder typical behavior, described by a power of log(1/epsilon). After incorporating SOL into a robustness certifier, they observe similar or higher certification rates and runtimes as low as one quarter of those of other methods. This provides empirical support for practicality despite the demanding worst-case bound.
neurips-2023-sol-sampling-based-optimal-.tldr: SOL adaptively samples Lipschitz-continuous functions to construct nearly optimal linear bounds, with practical gains demonstrated in robustness certification.

paragraphs: Many quantum-machine-learning applications can be viewed as learning a quantum state that represents useful data. Starting from a state already close to the target might appear to make this easier. This paper develops a no-go result showing a limitation of that strategy for quantum neural networks, even with a high-fidelity initial state.

The key condition is that the loss falls below a critical threshold. In that regime, the probability of avoiding local minima decreases exponentially with the number of qubits, while increasing only polynomially with circuit depth. The authors also characterize the curvature around local minima through the quantum Fisher information, scaled by a loss-dependent constant. This relates the local optimization landscape to the output state's sensitivity to network parameters.

The stated results cover arbitrary circuit structures and initialization strategies, including fixed and adaptive approaches. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical findings. Their significance is a conditional scalability barrier: favorable initialization and adaptation face generic limits in the analyzed low-loss regime, so proximity to a target state does not by itself resolve the learning difficulty.
neurips-2023-statistical-analysis-of-qua.tldr: Below a critical loss threshold, quantum-state learning faces an exponentially worsening probability of avoiding local minima as qubit count grows.

paragraphs: Predicting how strongly a protein binds a ligand is important for computational drug discovery. Supervised methods depend on measured affinities, which are less available for some ligand classes, including antibodies. This paper instead learns from unlabeled protein-ligand complexes by reformulating binding-energy prediction as a generative modeling problem.

The authors train an energy-based model using denoising score matching over three-dimensional rotations and translations, then interpret its log-likelihood as binding affinity. Their central component is Neural Euler's Rotation Equations, or NERE, an equivariant network for predicting rotations. It models forces and torques between protein and ligand atoms, defining force through the gradient of an energy function with respect to atomic coordinates.

Evaluations cover protein-ligand and antibody-antigen affinity prediction. NERE outperforms all compared unsupervised baselines, including physics-based potentials and protein language models, in both cases. It also surpasses the supervised baselines in the antibody setting. These results support the proposed use of unlabeled structural complexes, especially for the evaluated setting where affinity labels are limited.
neurips-2023-unsupervised-protein-ligand.tldr: NERE learns binding-affinity predictions from unlabeled complexes using an energy model and force-and-torque-based rotation prediction.

paragraphs: Probabilistic time-series models predict distributions over future outcomes, making explanation more involved than identifying the inputs behind a single number. This paper develops a post hoc framework for identifying observed timesteps that appear salient to such a model. It connects those explanations to counterfactual reasoning about why a particular future was forecast.

The framework draws on a social-science account of explanation and an information-theoretic definition of saliency grounded in preattentive visual cognition. The authors extend that definition to multivariate forecasting and derive closed-form expressions for commonly used probability densities. This provides a principled basis for highlighting past observations associated with the model's probabilistic predictions.

The authors validate the method using synthetic data, where ground-truth saliency can be established. They then demonstrate applications with real-world data and forecasting models. Those examples show how the explanations can help domain experts formulate new hypotheses about causal relationships between features. The role is to support hypothesis formation; the stated real-world findings do not establish that salient observations are themselves proven causes.
neurips-2023-why-did-this-model-forecast.tldr: An information-theoretic saliency framework identifies past timesteps relevant to probabilistic forecasts and helps experts formulate counterfactual and causal hypotheses.
